statement: If real functions $f$ and $g$ are [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at a point $x$, then their [product](c:product-of-functions) $fg$ is differentiable at $x$, and its [derivative](c:derivative) is $(fg)'(x) = f'(x)\,g(x) + f(x)\,g'(x)$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at $x$.
The function $g$ is [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at $x$.

conclusion: The product $fg$ is differentiable at $x$, and $(fg)'(x) = f'(x)\,g(x) + f(x)\,g'(x)$.

formal.difference: The declaration treats Fréchet derivatives of functions from a normed space to a commutative normed algebra. It states only the formula; the differentiability of the product is a separate declaration.

proofs.name: Bilinear map and chain rule
proofs.slogan: Write the product as the bilinear multiplication map applied to the pair $(f, g)$, and differentiate the composite by the chain rule.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for real functions. The same steps work for functions with values in any commutative normed algebra.

roles.why: Differentiability of $f$ gives the first coordinate of the derivative of the pair map.
Differentiability of $g$ gives the second coordinate of the derivative of the pair map.

steps.slogan: Combine $f$ and $g$ into the pair map $F(t) = (f(t), g(t))$.
steps.detail: The map $F$ into $\mathbb{R}^2$ is differentiable at $x$ with derivative $h \mapsto (f'(x)h, g'(x)h)$, because each coordinate is differentiable at $x$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the [bilinear map](c:bilinear-map) $B(u, v) = uv$ at the point $(p, q)$.
steps.detail: $B(p + h, q + k) - B(p, q) = pk + hq + hk$. The rest term satisfies $|hk| \le \|(h, k)\|^2$, so it is $o(\|(h, k)\|)$, and $B'(p, q)(h, k) = pk + hq$.

steps.slogan: Compose the derivative of $B$ with the derivative of $F$ by the chain rule.
steps.detail: Since $fg = B \circ F$, the chain rule makes $fg$ differentiable at $x$ with derivative $h \mapsto B'(F(x))(F'(x)h) = f(x)\,g'(x)\,h + f'(x)\,h\,g(x)$.

steps.slogan: Read the coefficient of $h$ as the [derivative](c:derivative) of $fg$ at $x$.
steps.detail: The derivative of $fg$ at $x$ is the number that multiplies $h$, which is $f'(x)\,g(x) + f(x)\,g'(x)$. Commutativity of multiplication puts the terms in this order.

concepts.c:differentiable-function: Both factors must have linear approximations at the point.
concepts.c:product-of-functions: The product is the composite of the pair map and multiplication.
concepts.c:derivative: The derivative of the composite is read as the coefficient of $h$.
concepts.c:bilinear-map: Multiplication is bilinear, so its derivative is explicit and its error is quadratic.

source.note: mathlib proves HasFDerivAt.mul' by IsBoundedBilinearMap.hasFDerivAt for ContinuousLinearMap.mul, composed (HasFDerivAt.comp) with the pair map from HasFDerivAt.prodMk.

proofs.name: Difference quotient
proofs.slogan: Split the difference quotient of $fg$ into two quotients by adding and subtracting $f(x+h)\,g(x)$, then pass to the limit.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for functions of one real variable. The limit is taken as $h \to 0$ with $h \neq 0$.

roles.why: It gives the limit $f'(x)$ and, through it, the continuity of $f$ at $x$.
It gives the limit $g'(x)$ of the second quotient.

steps.slogan: Add and subtract $f(x+h)\,g(x)$ in the numerator of the difference quotient.
steps.detail: For $h \neq 0$, the added and subtracted terms cancel, so $\frac{f(x+h)g(x+h) - f(x)g(x)}{h} = f(x+h)\,\frac{g(x+h) - g(x)}{h} + g(x)\,\frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}$. Each quotient on the right has a known limit.

steps.slogan: Derive the continuity of $f$ at $x$ from its differentiability.
steps.detail: $f(x+h) - f(x) = h \cdot \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}$ tends to $0 \cdot f'(x) = 0$ as $h \to 0$, so $f(x+h) \to f(x)$.

steps.slogan: Take the [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) of each term of the split as $h \to 0$.
steps.detail: The limit of a product is the product of the limits: $f(x+h) \to f(x)$, the quotient of $g$ tends to $g'(x)$ and the quotient of $f$ tends to $f'(x)$. So the quotient of $fg$ tends to $f(x)\,g'(x) + g(x)\,f'(x)$.

concepts.c:differentiable-function: Differentiability gives the two limits and the continuity of $f$.
concepts.c:product-of-functions: The product's difference quotient is split into two simpler quotients.
concepts.c:derivative: The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-function: Limits of products and sums give the limit of the split quotient.

source.note: The classical proof by adding and subtracting a term, as in Spivak, Calculus, chapter 10.

statement: If $f$ is a [measurable](c:measurable-function) [nonnegative function](c:nonnegative-function) on a [measure space](c:measure-space) $(X, \mu)$ and $0 < t < \infty$, then $t\,\mu(\{x : f(x) \ge t\}) \le \int_X f\,d\mu$, so $\mu(\{f \ge t\}) \le \frac{1}{t}\int_X f\,d\mu$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [measurable](c:measurable-function) on the measure space $(X, \mu)$.
The function $f$ is [nonnegative](c:nonnegative-function), with values in $[0, \infty]$.
The level $t$ satisfies $0 < t < \infty$.

conclusion: $t\,\mu(\{f \ge t\}) \le \int_X f\,d\mu$, and hence $\mu(\{f \ge t\}) \le \frac{1}{t}\int_X f\,d\mu$.

formal.difference: The declaration states only the multiplied form $\varepsilon\,\mu\{\varepsilon \le f\} \le \int f\,d\mu$, for every $\varepsilon \in [0, \infty]$. The divided form needs $0 < t < \infty$.

proofs.name: Step function below the function
proofs.slogan: Bound $f$ from below by $t$ times the indicator of the set where $f \ge t$, and integrate both sides.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $\int_X f\,d\mu = \infty$, both forms hold trivially, and the proof needs no separate case.

roles.why: Measurability makes the level set measurable, so $\mu(A)$ and the integral of its indicator exist.
Nonnegativity gives $t\,\mathbf{1}_A \le f$ outside the level set.
A finite positive level can be divided out of the inequality.

steps.slogan: Define the level set $A = \{x : f(x) \ge t\}$ and check that it is measurable.
steps.detail: $A$ is the preimage of the closed ray $[t, \infty]$ under the [measurable](c:measurable-function) map $f$. So $A$ is a measurable set and $\mu(A)$ is defined.

steps.slogan: Compare $f$ pointwise with the step function $t\,\mathbf{1}_A$.
steps.detail: On $A$, $t\,\mathbf{1}_A(x) = t \le f(x)$. Outside $A$, $t\,\mathbf{1}_A(x) = 0 \le f(x)$ because $f$ is [nonnegative](c:nonnegative-function). So $t\,\mathbf{1}_A \le f$ everywhere.

steps.slogan: Integrate both sides and use the monotonicity of the [integral](c:lebesgue-integral).
steps.detail: The integral of the simple function $t\,\mathbf{1}_A$ is $t\,\mu(A)$. The integral of nonnegative functions is monotone, so $t\,\mu(A) \le \int_X f\,d\mu$.

steps.slogan: Divide the inequality by the positive number $t$.
steps.detail: Because $0 < t < \infty$, division by $t$ keeps the inequality, also when the integral is infinite. This gives $\mu(A) \le \frac{1}{t}\int_X f\,d\mu$.

concepts.c:measurable-function: Measurability makes the level set measurable and the integrals defined.
concepts.c:nonnegative-function: Nonnegativity keeps the step function below $f$ off the level set.
concepts.c:measure-space: The measure gives the size of the level set that the bound controls.
concepts.c:lebesgue-integral: Monotonicity of the integral turns the pointwise bound into the inequality.

source.note: mathlib applies lintegral_add_mul_meas_add_le_le_lintegral with the zero function: the indicator of the level set times ε lies below f (lintegral_mono), and setLIntegral_const computes its integral.

statement: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group) and $k$ a field whose [characteristic](c:characteristic) does not divide $|G|$. Every [subrepresentation](c:subrepresentation) $W$ of a [representation](c:group-representation) $V$ of $G$ over $k$ has a $G$-invariant complement, so every finite-dimensional representation is a [direct sum](c:direct-sum) of [irreducible representations](c:irreducible-representation).

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is [finite](c:finite-group).
The [characteristic](c:characteristic) of $k$ does not divide $|G|$, so $|G|$ is invertible in $k$.
For the decomposition, the representation $V$ is finite dimensional over $k$.

conclusion: Every subrepresentation $W \subseteq V$ has a subrepresentation $W'$ with $V = W \oplus W'$, and a finite-dimensional $V$ is a direct sum of irreducible subrepresentations.

formal.difference: The declaration gives the invariant complement for every $k[G]$-module, finite dimensional or not, but not the decomposition into irreducible representations. It states the characteristic condition as $|G| \neq 0$ in $k$.

proofs.name: Averaged projection
proofs.slogan: Average a linear projection onto $W$ over the group to get a $G$-linear projection, and take its kernel as the invariant complement.
proofs.scope: The complement for every representation, then the decomposition by induction on the dimension. The zero representation is the empty direct sum.

roles.why: Finiteness of $G$ makes the average a finite sum of $|G|$ terms.
The characteristic condition lets the proof divide by $|G|$.
Finite dimension makes the induction on the dimension end.

steps.slogan: Choose a $k$-linear [projection](c:projection) $\pi\colon V \to W$ that fixes every vector of $W$.
steps.detail: Every subspace of a vector space has a linear complement, so $V = W \oplus U$ as vector spaces. The projection along $U$ is a $k$-linear map $\pi$ with $\pi(w) = w$ for $w \in W$.

steps.slogan: Average the conjugates of $\pi$ over the group to form the map $\pi^\circ$.
steps.detail: Set $\pi^\circ(v) = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} g^{-1}\pi(g v)$. The sum is finite because $G$ is finite, and $1/|G|$ exists because the characteristic of $k$ does not divide $|G|$.

steps.slogan: Reindex the sum to show that $\pi^\circ$ commutes with the group action.
steps.detail: For $h \in G$, $\pi^\circ(hv) = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g g^{-1}\pi(ghv)$. The substitution $g' = gh$ turns this into $h\,\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g'} g'^{-1}\pi(g'v) = h\,\pi^\circ(v)$.

steps.slogan: Check that $\pi^\circ$ still fixes every vector of $W$.
steps.detail: For $w \in W$, $gw \in W$ because $W$ is a [subrepresentation](c:subrepresentation), so $g^{-1}\pi(gw) = g^{-1}gw = w$. The $|G|$ equal terms give $\pi^\circ(w) = w$.

steps.slogan: Take the kernel of $\pi^\circ$ as the $G$-invariant complement of $W$.
steps.detail: The map $\pi^\circ$ has image in $W$ and fixes $W$, so it is a projection onto $W$ and $V = W \oplus \ker \pi^\circ$. The kernel of a $G$-linear map is $G$-invariant.

steps.slogan: Split $V$ again and again by induction on its dimension.
steps.detail:
If $V 
eq 0$ is not irreducible, it has a subrepresentation $0 
eq W 
eq V$, and $V = W \oplus W'$ with both parts of smaller dimension. The induction hypothesis writes $W$ and $W'$ as direct sums of irreducible representations, so $V$ is one too.

concepts.c:finite-group: Only a finite group can be averaged over by a finite sum.
concepts.c:characteristic: The average divides by $|G|$, which must be nonzero in $k$.
concepts.c:subrepresentation: Invariance of $W$ makes the averaged map fix $W$.
concepts.c:group-representation: The group acts linearly, so the conjugates $g^{-1}\pi g$ are linear maps.
concepts.c:direct-sum: The complement splits the representation as a direct sum.
concepts.c:irreducible-representation: Irreducible pieces are where the repeated splitting stops.
concepts.c:projection: A projection fixing $W$ has a kernel complementary to $W$.

statement: If $a < b$ and $f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $[a, b]$ and [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) on $(a, b)$, then some $c \in (a, b)$ has [derivative](c:derivative) $f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$.

hypotheses.text: The endpoints satisfy $a < b$.
The function $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on the closed interval $[a, b]$.
The function $f$ is [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at every point of the open interval $(a, b)$.

proofs.name: Auxiliary function and Rolle's theorem
proofs.slogan: Tilt $f$ by a multiple of $x$ to get a function with equal end values, and find a stationary point of it by Rolle's theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The hypothesis $a < b$ makes the open interval nonempty and the slope defined.

roles.why: It gives a nondegenerate interval for Rolle's theorem and a nonzero denominator $b - a$.
Continuity of $f$ makes the auxiliary function continuous on $[a, b]$.
Differentiability of $f$ makes the auxiliary function differentiable on $(a, b)$ and gives its derivative.

steps.slogan: Define the auxiliary function $h(x) = (b - a)\,f(x) - (f(b) - f(a))\,x$.
steps.detail: The function $h$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$ with $h'(x) = (b - a)f'(x) - (f(b) - f(a))$, because it is a linear combination of $f$ and the identity.

steps.slogan: Compare the end values $h(a)$ and $h(b)$ of the auxiliary function.
Find a point $c \in (a, b)$ with $h'(c) = 0$ by Rolle's theorem.
steps.detail: Rolle's theorem applies to $h$ on $[a, b]$: $a < b$, $h$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, differentiable on $(a, b)$, and $h(a) = h(b)$.

steps.slogan: Solve the equation $h'(c) = 0$ for the [derivative](c:derivative) $f'(c)$.
steps.detail: $h'(c) = 0$ means $(b - a)\,f'(c) = f(b) - f(a)$. Division by $b - a \neq 0$ gives $f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity on the closed interval passes to the auxiliary function for Rolle.
concepts.c:differentiable-function: Differentiability inside the interval gives the derivative of the auxiliary function.
concepts.c:derivative: The stationary point of the auxiliary function gives the required derivative value.

statement: On a [measure space](c:measure-space) $(X, \mu)$, for $1 \le p < \infty$ and [measurable](c:measurable-function) functions $f, g\colon X \to [0, \infty]$, the [Lp norm](c:lp-norm) $\|f\|_p = (\int_X f^p\,d\mu)^{1/p}$ satisfies $\|f + g\|_p \le \|f\|_p + \|g\|_p$.

hypotheses.text: The exponent satisfies $1 \le p < \infty$.
The functions $f$ and $g$ are [measurable](c:measurable-function), with values in $[0, \infty]$.

formal.difference: The declaration needs only almost-everywhere measurability of $f$ and $g$; otherwise it states the same inequality.

proofs.name: Hölder on a split power
proofs.slogan: Split $(f + g)^p$ as $f(f + g)^{p-1} + g(f + g)^{p-1}$, bound each part by Hölder's inequality, and divide by the common factor.
proofs.scope: The main case $p > 1$ with $0 < \int (f + g)^p < \infty$; step 1 settles the other cases. Real or complex functions follow from $|f + g| \le |f| + |g|$.

roles.why: The exponent $p > 1$ has a conjugate exponent $q$, and $p \ge 1$ makes $t \mapsto t^p$ convex.
Measurability makes the integrals defined and additive.

steps.slogan: Settle the cases of an infinite right side, $p = 1$ and $\int (f + g)^p = 0$.
steps.detail: An infinite right side or a zero left side makes the inequality trivial, and for $p = 1$ additivity of the integral gives equality. Otherwise $p > 1$, and $q = p/(p - 1)$ satisfies $1/p + 1/q = 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\int (f + g)^p$ is finite by the [convexity](c:convex-function) of $t \mapsto t^p$.
steps.detail: Convexity gives $(a + b)^p \le 2^{p-1}(a^p + b^p)$ for $a, b \ge 0$. Integration bounds $\int (f + g)^p$ by $2^{p-1}(\int f^p + \int g^p)$, which is finite in the main case.

steps.slogan: Split the integrand as $(f + g)^p = f\,(f + g)^{p-1} + g\,(f + g)^{p-1}$.
steps.detail: The identity holds pointwise. Additivity of the integral of [measurable](c:measurable-function) nonnegative functions gives $\int (f + g)^p = \int f(f + g)^{p-1} + \int g(f + g)^{p-1}$.

steps.slogan: Bound each part of the split by Hölder's inequality with exponents $p$ and $q$.
steps.detail: Hölder gives $\int f(f + g)^{p-1} \le \|f\|_p\,(\int (f + g)^{(p-1)q})^{1/q}$, and $(p - 1)q = p$. The same bound for $g$ gives $\int (f + g)^p \le (\|f\|_p + \|g\|_p)(\int (f + g)^p)^{1/q}$.

steps.slogan: Divide by the finite nonzero factor $(\int (f + g)^p)^{1/q}$.
steps.detail: Since $1 - 1/q = 1/p$, the division gives $(\int (f + g)^p)^{1/p} \le \|f\|_p + \|g\|_p$, which is the inequality of [Lp norms](c:lp-norm).

concepts.c:measure-space: The integrals that define the norms are taken over this measure.
concepts.c:measurable-function: Measurability makes the integrals exist and add.
concepts.c:lp-norm: The inequality is the triangle inequality of this norm.
concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity of $t^p$ shows that the left side is finite before the division.

source.note: mathlib settles the trivial cases, proves finiteness by lintegral_rpow_add_lt_top_of_lintegral_rpow_lt_top, and bounds the split integral by Hölder (lintegral_rpow_add_le_add_eLpNorm_mul_lintegral_rpow_add) in lintegral_Lp_add_le_aux.

statement: A language $L$ of [words](c:word) over an alphabet $\Sigma$ is [regular](c:regular-language) if and only if the Myhill–Nerode [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation), $u \sim v$ when $uw \in L \Leftrightarrow vw \in L$ for every word $w$, has finitely many classes, that is, iff $L$ has finitely many left quotients $u^{-1}L = \{w : uw \in L\}$.

hypotheses.text: The set $L$ consists of finite [words](c:word) over an alphabet $\Sigma$.

conclusion: $L$ is accepted by a [deterministic finite automaton](c:dfa) exactly when $\sim$ has finitely many classes.

formal.difference: The declaration counts the left quotients $u^{-1}L$ instead of the classes of $\sim$. The two counts agree because $u \sim v$ means $u^{-1}L = v^{-1}L$.

proofs.name: Left quotients as states
proofs.slogan: A finite automaton has at most one left quotient per state, and conversely the left quotients themselves are the states of an automaton for $L$.
proofs.scope: Both directions, for any alphabet. The empty language has the single left quotient $\emptyset$ and is regular.

roles.why: Words over $\Sigma$ are the inputs whose left quotients the proof compares.

steps.slogan: Match the classes of $\sim$ with the left quotients of $L$.
steps.detail: By definition $u \sim v$ holds exactly when $u^{-1}L = v^{-1}L$. So $u \mapsto u^{-1}L$ is a bijection from the classes of the [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation) onto the set of left quotients.

steps.slogan: Show that in an automaton for $L$ the state after $u$ determines $u^{-1}L$.
steps.detail: Let a [DFA](c:dfa) $M$ with finite state set $Q$ accept $L$, and let $\delta(u)$ be its state after reading $u$. Then $uw \in L$ iff $M$ accepts $w$ from $\delta(u)$, so $u^{-1}L$ depends only on $\delta(u)$, and there are at most $|Q|$ left quotients.

steps.slogan: Build an automaton whose states are the left quotients of $L$.
steps.detail: Take the start state $L$, the transition $(K, a) \mapsto a^{-1}K$ and the accepting states $K$ that contain the empty word. The transitions stay in the set because $a^{-1}(u^{-1}L) = (ua)^{-1}L$, and finitely many quotients make the automaton finite.

steps.slogan: Show by induction on the length of $w$ that the automaton reaches $w^{-1}L$.
steps.detail: Reading $a$ in the state $w^{-1}L$ leads to $a^{-1}(w^{-1}L) = (wa)^{-1}L$. So the automaton accepts $w$ iff the empty word lies in $w^{-1}L$, that is, iff $w \in L$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions with the bijection of step 1.
steps.detail: Step 2 shows that a [regular](c:regular-language) $L$ has finitely many left quotients, and steps 3 and 4 give a finite automaton for $L$ from finitely many quotients. Step 1 turns the count of quotients into the count of classes of $\sim$.

concepts.c:word: Quotients and automaton runs are defined by reading words letter by letter.
concepts.c:regular-language: Regularity means acceptance by a finite automaton, the property characterized.
concepts.c:equivalence-relation: The classes of the Myhill–Nerode relation are what the theorem counts.
concepts.c:dfa: Automaton states bound the quotients, and quotients become automaton states.

statement: Let $H$ be a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) of dimension at least 2 and $e \in H$ a unit vector. No [unitary operator](c:unitary-operator) $U$ on the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) $H \otimes H$ copies every [quantum state](c:quantum-state): some unit vector $\psi \in H$ has $U(\psi \otimes e) \neq \psi \otimes \psi$.

hypotheses.text: The [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ has dimension at least 2.
The operator $U$ on $H \otimes H$ is [unitary](c:unitary-operator), and the blank state $e \in H$ is a fixed unit vector.

conclusion: Some unit vector $\psi \in H$ has $U(\psi \otimes e) \neq \psi \otimes \psi$.

proofs.name: Inner products before and after
proofs.slogan: A unitary copier keeps inner products, but copying squares them, so two copied states are equal or orthogonal.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by contradiction. In dimension 1 every state is a multiple of one vector, and copying is possible, so the dimension bound is needed.

roles.why: It gives two unit vectors that are neither equal nor orthogonal.
Unitarity keeps inner products, which gives the equation of step 4.

steps.slogan: Assume that $U$ copies every unit vector, and choose two test states.
steps.detail: Since $\dim H \ge 2$, take orthonormal $u, v$ and set $\psi = u$ and $\varphi = (u + v)/\sqrt{2}$. These unit vectors have $\langle \varphi, \psi \rangle = 1/\sqrt{2}$.

steps.slogan: Compute the inner product of the inputs $\varphi \otimes e$ and $\psi \otimes e$.
steps.detail: The inner product of simple vectors in a [tensor product](c:tensor-product) factors: $\langle \varphi \otimes e, \psi \otimes e \rangle = \langle \varphi, \psi \rangle \langle e, e \rangle = \langle \varphi, \psi \rangle$.

steps.slogan: Compute the inner product of the outputs $\varphi \otimes \varphi$ and $\psi \otimes \psi$.
steps.detail: The outputs have $\langle \varphi \otimes \varphi, \psi \otimes \psi \rangle = \langle \varphi, \psi \rangle^2$. A [unitary operator](c:unitary-operator) keeps inner products, so this equals the inner product of the inputs.

steps.slogan: Solve $\langle \varphi, \psi \rangle = \langle \varphi, \psi \rangle^2$ and contradict the choice of states.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give $\langle \varphi, \psi \rangle = \langle \varphi, \psi \rangle^2$, so $\langle \varphi, \psi \rangle \in \{0, 1\}$. The chosen states have $\langle \varphi, \psi \rangle = 1/\sqrt{2}$, so $U$ fails to copy $\psi$ or $\varphi$.

concepts.c:hilbert-space: The inner product of the Hilbert space is the quantity that copying breaks.
concepts.c:unitary-operator: Unitarity keeps inner products between input and output states.
concepts.c:tensor-product: Inner products of simple tensors factor into products of inner products.
concepts.c:quantum-state: The states to copy are unit vectors of $H$.

source.note: The inner product proof, as in Nielsen and Chuang, Quantum Computation and Quantum Information (2000), chapter 12.

proofs.name: Linearity on a superposition
proofs.slogan: Copy two orthonormal states, then compare the linear image of their superposition with the copy of the superposition.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by contradiction. The proof uses only the linearity of $U$, so no linear map copies every state.

roles.why: It gives two orthonormal states to superpose.
Only the [linearity](c:linearity) of the unitary operator $U$ is used.

steps.slogan: Choose orthonormal vectors $u, v \in H$ and assume that $U$ copies every state.
steps.detail: Orthonormal $u, v$ exist since $\dim H \ge 2$. If $U$ copies every state, then $U(u \otimes e) = u \otimes u$ and $U(v \otimes e) = v \otimes v$.

steps.slogan: Apply $U$ to the superposition $\chi = (u + v)/\sqrt{2}$ by linearity.
steps.detail: Since $\chi \otimes e = (u \otimes e + v \otimes e)/\sqrt{2}$, [linearity](c:linearity) gives $U(\chi \otimes e) = (u \otimes u + v \otimes v)/\sqrt{2}$.

steps.slogan: Expand the required copy $\chi \otimes \chi$ in the product basis.
steps.detail: Bilinearity of the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) gives $\chi \otimes \chi = \frac12(u \otimes u + u \otimes v + v \otimes u + v \otimes v)$, whose coefficient on $u \otimes v$ is $\frac12$.

steps.slogan: Compare the coefficients of $u \otimes v$ in the two vectors.
steps.detail: The vectors $u \otimes u$, $u \otimes v$, $v \otimes u$ and $v \otimes v$ are orthonormal in $H \otimes H$. The coefficient of $u \otimes v$ is $0$ in step 2 and $\frac12$ in step 3, so $U(\chi \otimes e) \neq \chi \otimes \chi$.

concepts.c:hilbert-space: Its dimension supplies two orthonormal states to superpose.
concepts.c:unitary-operator: The copier is unitary, but the proof needs only its linearity.
concepts.c:tensor-product: Copying is quadratic in the state inside the tensor product.
concepts.c:quantum-state: The superposition $\chi$ is itself a state that a copier must copy.
concepts.c:linearity: Linearity forces the image of a superposition, which differs from its copy.

source.note: The linearity argument of W. K. Wootters and W. H. Zurek, A single quantum cannot be cloned, Nature 299 (1982), 802-803.

statement: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group) and $k$ an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field) whose characteristic does not divide $|G|$. For [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation) finite-dimensional representations $V, W$ of $G$ over $k$, the [characters](c:character-of-a-representation) satisfy $\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} \chi_V(g)\,\chi_W(g^{-1}) = 1$ if $V \cong W$ and $0$ otherwise.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is [finite](c:finite-group).
The field $k$ is [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field).
The characteristic of $k$ does not divide $|G|$.
The representations $V$ and $W$ are finite dimensional and [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation).

conclusion: $\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} \chi_V(g)\,\chi_W(g^{-1})$ equals $1$ when $V \cong W$ and $0$ otherwise.

proofs.name: Dimension of invariant maps
proofs.slogan: Read the sum as the average character of $G$ acting on $\operatorname{Hom}_k(W, V)$, which counts the invariant maps, and count them by Schur's lemma.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The equality holds in $k$, where $0$ and $1$ are images of dimensions; in characteristic 0 it is an equality of numbers.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the sum over $G$ and the averaging operator finite.
Algebraic closure makes every $G$-endomorphism of an irreducible representation a scalar.
It makes $1/|G|$ exist in $k$, so the averaging operator is defined.
Finite dimension makes traces defined, and irreducibility makes Schur's lemma apply.

steps.slogan: Compute the [character](c:character-of-a-representation) of $G$ acting on $\operatorname{Hom}_k(W, V)$.
steps.detail: Let $g$ act by $f \mapsto g f g^{-1}$. Since $\operatorname{Hom}_k(W, V) \cong W^* \otimes V$, its character is $\chi_W(g^{-1})\,\chi_V(g)$, the product of the dual and the tensor characters.

steps.slogan: Average the action over $G$ to get a projection onto the invariant maps.
steps.detail: The operator $P = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g g$ exists because $|G|$ is invertible in $k$. It fixes every invariant map and has its image in the invariants, so it is a projection onto $\operatorname{Hom}_G(W, V)$.

steps.slogan: Take the trace of the projection $P$ to count the invariant maps.
steps.detail: The trace of a projection is the dimension of its image. By step 1 the trace of $P$ is $\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g \chi_V(g)\chi_W(g^{-1})$, so this sum equals $\dim_k \operatorname{Hom}_G(W, V)$ in $k$.

steps.slogan: Count the invariant maps between the irreducible representations by Schur's lemma.
steps.detail: A nonzero $G$-map between [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation) representations is an isomorphism, so $\operatorname{Hom}_G(W, V) = 0$ if $V \not\cong W$. Over an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field) $\operatorname{End}_G(V) = k$, so the dimension is 1 if $V \cong W$.

concepts.c:finite-group: The average over a finite group is a finite sum.
concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: Algebraic closure makes the endomorphisms of an irreducible representation scalars.
concepts.c:irreducible-representation: Schur's lemma needs irreducible representations on both sides.
concepts.c:character-of-a-representation: Characters turn the count of invariant maps into a trace computation.

source.note: mathlib rewrites the sum by scalar_product_char_eq_finrank_equivariant (char_linHom and average_char_eq_finrank_invariants, the trace of the averaging projection) and finishes with Schur's lemma finrank_hom_simple_simple.

statement: For a [linear map](c:linear-map) $f\colon V \to W$ between [vector spaces](c:vector-space) over a field, with $V$ [finite dimensional](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space), $\dim V = \dim \ker f + \dim \operatorname{im} f$: the [dimension](c:dimension-of-a-vector-space) of $V$ is the sum of the dimensions of the [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) and the [image](c:image).

hypotheses.text: The map $f\colon V \to W$ is [linear](c:linear-map) over a field $K$.
The domain $V$ is [finite dimensional](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space).

formal.difference: The declaration states the equality of cardinal ranks for every vector space, finite dimensional or not, and for modules over any ring with the rank-nullity property.

proofs.name: Quotient by the kernel
proofs.slogan: Identify the image with the quotient by the kernel, and split the domain as the product of the quotient and the kernel.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $f = 0$, the kernel is $V$ and the image is $0$, and the steps still apply.

roles.why: Linearity makes the kernel a subspace and the induced map on the quotient linear.
Finite dimension makes all the dimensions finite numbers that add as integers.

steps.slogan: Identify the image with the quotient $V/\ker f$ by the first isomorphism theorem.
steps.detail: The map $v + \ker f \mapsto f(v)$ is well defined, linear and injective, and its image is $\operatorname{im} f$. So $V/\ker f \cong \operatorname{im} f$, and the two spaces have the same [dimension](c:dimension-of-a-vector-space).

steps.slogan: Choose a complement $U$ of $\ker f$ and identify it with the quotient.
steps.detail: Every subspace has a complement, so $V = \ker f \oplus U$. The quotient map restricts to an isomorphism $U \cong V/\ker f$, so $V \cong (V/\ker f) \times \ker f$.

steps.slogan: Add the dimensions of the two factors of the product.
steps.detail: A [basis](c:basis) of $V/\ker f$ and a basis of $\ker f$ together give a basis of the product. So $\dim V = \dim(V/\ker f) + \dim \ker f$, and all three numbers are finite.

steps.slogan: Replace the quotient by the image in the dimension count.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives $\dim(V/\ker f) = \dim \operatorname{im} f$. Substitution in step 3 gives $\dim V = \dim \operatorname{im} f + \dim \ker f$.

concepts.c:linear-map: Linearity gives the kernel, the image and the induced isomorphism.
concepts.c:vector-space: Over a field every subspace has a complement.
concepts.c:finite-dimensional-vector-space: Finite dimension makes the dimension count an equation of integers.
concepts.c:dimension-of-a-vector-space: Isomorphic spaces have equal dimension, and dimensions of products add.
concepts.c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism: The kernel is the subspace divided out and counted.
concepts.c:image: The image is isomorphic to the quotient by the kernel.
concepts.c:basis: Joined bases of the two factors give a basis of the product.

source.note: mathlib uses quotKerEquivRange (first isomorphism theorem) and rank_quotient_add_rank, which over a division ring comes from quotient_prod_linearEquiv (a complement) and rank_prod'.

proofs.name: Extension of a kernel basis
proofs.slogan: Extend a basis of the kernel to a basis of $V$, and show that the images of the new vectors form a basis of the image.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $\ker f = 0$ the kernel basis is empty, and if $f = 0$ no new vectors appear.

roles.why: Linearity gives $f(v) = \sum b_j f(v_j)$ and moves a relation among images into the kernel.
Finite dimension gives finite bases to extend and count.

steps.slogan: Extend a basis $u_1, \dots, u_k$ of $\ker f$ to a basis $u_1, \dots, u_k, v_1, \dots, v_r$ of $V$.
steps.detail: A linearly independent list in a finite-dimensional space extends to a [basis](c:basis), by the exchange lemma. So $\dim V = k + r$ with $k = \dim \ker f$.

steps.slogan: Show that the vectors $f(v_1), \dots, f(v_r)$ span the image.
steps.detail: Write $v = \sum a_i u_i + \sum b_j v_j$. Since $f(u_i) = 0$, $f(v) = \sum b_j f(v_j)$, so every vector of $\operatorname{im} f$ is a combination of the $f(v_j)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the vectors $f(v_1), \dots, f(v_r)$ are linearly independent.
steps.detail: If $\sum b_j f(v_j) = 0$, then $\sum b_j v_j \in \ker f$, so $\sum b_j v_j = \sum a_i u_i$ for some $a_i$. Independence of the whole basis forces every $b_j = 0$.

steps.slogan: Count the vectors of the two bases to get the formula.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 make $f(v_1), \dots, f(v_r)$ a basis of $\operatorname{im} f$, so $\dim \operatorname{im} f = r$. Then $\dim V = k + r = \dim \ker f + \dim \operatorname{im} f$.

concepts.c:linear-map: Linearity sends the kernel basis to zero and keeps combinations.
concepts.c:vector-space: Bases and their extensions exist in vector spaces over a field.
concepts.c:finite-dimensional-vector-space: Finite bases make the count a sum of integers.
concepts.c:dimension-of-a-vector-space: The dimension is the number of vectors in a basis.
concepts.c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism: The kernel basis is the start of the extended basis.
concepts.c:image: The images of the new basis vectors form a basis of the image.
concepts.c:basis: The proof counts the vectors of an extended basis.

source.note: The basis-extension proof, as in Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, theorem 3.22 (fundamental theorem of linear maps).

statement: Every nonempty [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space) [open set](c:open-set) $U \subsetneq \mathbb{C}$ has a [biholomorphic](c:biholomorphic-function) map $f$ onto the [unit disc](c:unit-disc) $D = \{z : |z| < 1\}$, and for a given $z_0 \in U$ one can take $f(z_0) = 0$.

hypotheses.text: The set $U$ is a nonempty [open set](c:open-set) in $\mathbb{C}$.
The set $U$ is [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space).
The set $U$ is not all of $\mathbb{C}$.

conclusion: There is a bijective [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) map $f\colon U \to D$ with holomorphic inverse and $f(z_0) = 0$.

proofs.name: Extremal problem for the derivative
proofs.slogan: Among injective holomorphic maps of $U$ into the disc that send $z_0$ to $0$, take one with the largest $|f'(z_0)|$ and show that it is onto.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by the Koebe extremal argument; the inverse is holomorphic because an injective holomorphic map has a nonvanishing derivative. The hypothesis $U \neq \mathbb{C}$ is necessary, because Liouville's theorem excludes a bounded nonconstant entire map.

roles.why: An open nonempty set carries holomorphic maps and a base point $z_0$.
Simple connectivity gives holomorphic square roots of nonvanishing functions.
A point $a \notin U$ makes $z - a$ nonvanishing, which starts the first square root.

steps.slogan: Map $U$ injectively into the disc by a square root and a Möbius map.
steps.detail: Pick $a \notin U$; on the simply connected $U$, $z - a$ has a holomorphic [square root](c:square-root) $h$, which is injective with $h(U) \cap (-h(U)) = \emptyset$. The open set $-h(U)$ contains a disc that $h(U)$ omits, so $r/(h - c)$, for its center $c$ and radius $r$, followed by a [Möbius transformation](c:moebius-transformation) of $D$ maps $U$ into $D$ with $z_0 \mapsto 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that the family $\mathcal{F}$ of such maps is a [normal family](c:normal-family).
steps.detail: $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of injective holomorphic $f\colon U \to D$ with $f(z_0) = 0$; step 1 makes it nonempty, and it is bounded by 1. Montel's theorem gives every sequence in $\mathcal{F}$ a subsequence that converges uniformly on compact sets.

steps.slogan: Take the limit $f$ of a maximizing sequence for $|f'(z_0)|$ and show that $f$ lies in $\mathcal{F}$.
steps.detail: Cauchy estimates bound $|f'(z_0)|$ on $\mathcal{F}$, and a convergent subsequence of a maximizing sequence has a limit $f$ with $|f'(z_0)| = \sup > 0$. So $f$ is not constant, Hurwitz's theorem makes it injective, and the maximum modulus principle gives $f(U) \subseteq D$.

steps.slogan: Assume that $f$ omits a point $w \in D$, and build a map $g \in \mathcal{F}$ from it.
steps.detail: Compose $f$ with the Möbius map $\varphi_w$ that sends $w$ to $0$, take a holomorphic square root of the nonvanishing result, and move the value at $z_0$ back to $0$. The new $g \in \mathcal{F}$ satisfies $f = \Phi \circ g$, where $\Phi\colon D \to D$ fixes $0$ and is not injective, so it is not a rotation.

steps.slogan: Contradict the maximality of $|f'(z_0)|$ by the Schwarz lemma.
steps.detail: The Schwarz lemma gives $|\Phi'(0)| < 1$, so $|f'(z_0)| = |\Phi'(0)|\,|g'(z_0)| < |g'(z_0)|$, against the choice of $f$. So $f$ is onto $D$, and it is the required [biholomorphic](c:biholomorphic-function) map.

concepts.c:simply-connected-space: Simple connectivity gives the square roots in steps 1 and 4.
concepts.c:open-set: The domain is open, so holomorphic maps on it make sense.
concepts.c:biholomorphic-function: The extremal map is the required biholomorphic map onto the disc.
concepts.c:unit-disc: The disc is the target, and its self-maps obey the Schwarz lemma.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: All maps of the family are holomorphic and injective.
concepts.c:square-root: Square roots enlarge the derivative and give the first embedding.
concepts.c:moebius-transformation: Disc automorphisms move chosen points to the origin.
concepts.c:normal-family: Normality gives a convergent maximizing subsequence.

source.note: The Koebe extremal proof, as in Ahlfors, Complex Analysis, chapter 6, and Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, chapter 14.

statement: Every [impartial game](c:impartial-game) $G$ under the normal play convention whose plays all end is equivalent to the [nim](c:nim) heap $*\mathcal{G}(G)$. Here the Grundy value $\mathcal{G}(G)$ is the [minimum excludant](c:mex) of the Grundy values of the options of $G$, and equivalence means that $G + *\mathcal{G}(G)$ is a win for the second player.

hypotheses.text: The game $G$ is [impartial](c:impartial-game): from every position both players have the same moves.
The option relation of $G$ is [well-founded](c:well-founded-relation), so every play ends, and the player who cannot move loses.

conclusion: The sum $G + *\mathcal{G}(G)$ is a second-player win, so $G$ is equivalent to the nim heap $*\mathcal{G}(G)$.

proofs.name: Induction with mex replies
proofs.slogan: By well-founded induction, answer every move in $G + *\mathcal{G}(G)$ with a move to a sum $H + *\mathcal{G}(H)$, which the induction hypothesis makes a second-player win.
proofs.scope: All impartial games whose plays end. With infinitely many options at a position the Grundy values are ordinals, and the same proof works.

roles.why: Both players have the same moves, so one value describes a position for either player and $G = -G$.
Well-foundedness makes the recursion and the induction valid, and normal play decides the end positions.

steps.slogan: Define the Grundy value by recursion over the options of a position.
steps.detail: Set $\mathcal{G}(G) = \operatorname{mex}\{\mathcal{G}(G') : G' \text{ an option of } G\}$, the least value that no option attains. The recursion is valid because the option relation is [well-founded](c:well-founded-relation), and a position with no move gets $\mathcal{G} = 0$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the equivalence $G \approx *n$ to a second-player win in $G + *n$.
steps.detail: Two normal-play games are equivalent when their difference is a second-player win. An [impartial game](c:impartial-game) is its own negative, so $G \approx *n$ holds when $G + *n$ is a second-player win.

steps.slogan: Answer a heap move from $*n$ to $*m$ with $m < n$ by a move in $G$.
steps.detail: Let $n = \mathcal{G}(G)$. Since $m < n$ and $n$ is the [minimum excludant](c:mex), some option $G'$ of $G$ has $\mathcal{G}(G') = m$, and the reply to $G' + *m$ reaches a sum of the form $H + *\mathcal{G}(H)$.

steps.slogan: Answer a move from $G$ to an option $G'$ according to the size of $m = \mathcal{G}(G')$.
steps.detail: Here $m \neq n$ by the definition of mex. If $m < n$, reduce the [nim](c:nim) heap to $*m$; if $m > n$, some option $G''$ of $G'$ has $\mathcal{G}(G'') = n$, so move to $G'' + *n$.

steps.slogan: Conclude by induction that every sum $H + *\mathcal{G}(H)$ is a second-player win.
steps.detail: Each reply in steps 3 and 4 reaches a sum $H + *\mathcal{G}(H)$ with $H$ a later position of $G$, which is a second-player win by the induction hypothesis. So the second player wins $G + *n$, and step 2 gives $G \approx *\mathcal{G}(G)$.

concepts.c:impartial-game: Impartiality makes each game its own negative, so sums replace differences.
concepts.c:nim: Nim heaps are the normal forms to which every impartial game reduces.
concepts.c:mex: The mex definition supplies the replies in both kinds of moves.
concepts.c:well-founded-relation: Well-foundedness justifies the recursive definition and the induction.

source.note: The standard proof, as in Conway, On Numbers and Games (1976), and Siegel, Combinatorial Game Theory (2013).

statement: Let $A$ be a unital [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra), $H$ a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) and $\varphi\colon A \to B(H)$ a [completely positive map](c:completely-positive-map). Then there are a Hilbert space $K$, a unital $*$-representation $\pi\colon A \to B(K)$ and a [bounded operator](c:bounded-operator) $V\colon H \to K$ with $\varphi(a) = V^*\pi(a)V$ for every $a \in A$ and $\|V\|^2 = \|\varphi(1)\|$.

hypotheses.text: The algebra $A$ is a unital [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra).
The linear map $\varphi\colon A \to B(H)$ into the bounded operators on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ is [completely positive](c:completely-positive-map).

conclusion: $\varphi(a) = V^*\pi(a)V$ for a unital $*$-representation $\pi$ of $A$ on a Hilbert space $K$ and a bounded $V\colon H \to K$ with $\|V\|^2 = \|\varphi(1)\|$.

proofs.name: Construction on the tensor product
proofs.slogan: Build $K$ from $A \otimes H$ with the inner product that $\varphi$ gives, let $A$ act by left multiplication, and embed $H$ through the unit of $A$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by an explicit construction. For $H = \mathbb{C}$ and a state $\varphi$ it is the [GNS construction](c:gns-construction).

roles.why: The unit gives the embedding $V\xi = [1 \otimes \xi]$ and a unital representation.
Complete positivity makes the form positive semidefinite and bounds left multiplication.

steps.slogan: Define a [sesquilinear form](c:sesquilinear-form) on $A \otimes H$ through $\varphi$.
steps.detail: Set $\langle a \otimes \xi, b \otimes \eta \rangle = \langle \xi, \varphi(a^*b)\eta \rangle_H$. For $x = \sum_i a_i \otimes \xi_i$, $\langle x, x \rangle = \sum_{i,j}\langle \xi_i, \varphi(a_i^*a_j)\xi_j \rangle \ge 0$, because $[a_i^*a_j] \ge 0$ in $M_n(A)$ and $\varphi$ is [completely positive](c:completely-positive-map).

steps.slogan: Divide out the null vectors and complete the quotient to a Hilbert space $K$.
steps.detail: The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for the positive semidefinite form shows that $N = \{x : \langle x, x \rangle = 0\}$ is a subspace. The quotient $(A \otimes H)/N$ is an inner product space, and its [completion](c:completion) is $K$.

steps.slogan: Let $A$ act on $K$ by left multiplication $\pi(a)[b \otimes \xi] = [ab \otimes \xi]$.
steps.detail: Since $a^*a \le \|a\|^2 1$, the matrix $[b_i^*(\|a\|^2 - a^*a)b_j]$ is positive, and complete positivity gives $\langle \pi(a)x, \pi(a)x \rangle \le \|a\|^2\langle x, x \rangle$. So $\pi(a)$ keeps $N$, extends to $K$, and $\pi$ is a unital $*$-homomorphism.

steps.slogan: Define the operator $V\xi = [1 \otimes \xi]$ and compute its norm.
steps.detail: $\|V\xi\|^2 = \langle \xi, \varphi(1)\xi \rangle$, so $V$ is a [bounded operator](c:bounded-operator). Because $\varphi(1) \ge 0$, $\|V\|^2 = \sup_{\|\xi\| = 1}\langle \xi, \varphi(1)\xi \rangle = \|\varphi(1)\|$.

steps.slogan: Check the factorization $V^*\pi(a)V = \varphi(a)$ on pairs of vectors.
steps.detail: For $\xi, \eta \in H$, $\langle \eta, V^*\pi(a)V\xi \rangle = \langle 1 \otimes \eta, a \otimes \xi \rangle = \langle \eta, \varphi(a)\xi \rangle$. This holds for all $\xi, \eta$, so $V^*\pi(a)V = \varphi(a)$.

concepts.c:c-star-algebra: Positivity of matrices over the C*-algebra drives every estimate.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: The new space $K$ is a Hilbert space built from $A$ and $H$.
concepts.c:completely-positive-map: Complete positivity makes the inner product positive and $\pi(a)$ bounded.
concepts.c:bounded-operator: The map $V$ is bounded with norm given by $\varphi(1)$.
concepts.c:gns-construction: The proof extends the GNS construction from states to operator values.
concepts.c:sesquilinear-form: The form on $A \otimes H$ is the starting inner product.
concepts.c:completion: Completion turns the quotient inner product space into a Hilbert space.

source.note: Stinespring's construction: W. F. Stinespring, Positive functions on C*-algebras, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 6 (1955), 211-216; also Paulsen, Completely Bounded Maps and Operator Algebras (2002), theorem 4.1.

statement: Every [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) $B$ is isomorphic to a field of sets: the map $h(a) = \{U : a \in U\}$ is an injective Boolean homomorphism from $B$ into the [power set](c:power-set) of the set $S(B)$ of [ultrafilters](c:ultrafilter) of $B$, and its image is the set of [clopen](c:clopen-subset) subsets of the [Stone space](c:stone-space) $S(B)$.

hypotheses.text: The structure $B$ is a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra).

conclusion: The map $h$ is an isomorphism of $B$ onto the field of clopen subsets of $S(B)$.

proofs.name: Sets of ultrafilters
proofs.slogan: Send each element to the set of ultrafilters that contain it, separate elements by the ultrafilter theorem, and identify the image by compactness.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem in ZF with the ultrafilter theorem. The trivial algebra $0 = 1$ has no ultrafilters and maps onto the field of subsets of the empty set.

roles.why: Complements and distributivity give the prime property of ultrafilters and the separating element.

steps.slogan: Check that $h$ turns meets, joins and complements into intersections, unions and complements.
steps.detail: An [ultrafilter](c:ultrafilter) contains $a \wedge b$ iff it contains $a$ and $b$, contains $a \vee b$ iff it contains $a$ or $b$, and contains exactly one of $a$ and $\neg a$. So $h(a \wedge b) = h(a) \cap h(b)$, $h(a \vee b) = h(a) \cup h(b)$ and $h(\neg a) = S(B) \setminus h(a)$.

steps.slogan: Separate two different elements by an ultrafilter from the ultrafilter theorem.
steps.detail:
If $a 
eq b$, then $a \wedge 
eg b 
eq 0$ or $b \wedge 
eg a 
eq 0$, say the first. The filter generated by $a \wedge 
eg b$ is proper, and the ultrafilter theorem extends it to an ultrafilter $U \in h(a) \setminus h(b)$.

steps.slogan: Give $S(B)$ the topology with base $\{h(a)\}$, and show that each $h(a)$ is clopen.
steps.detail: The sets $h(a)$ are closed under finite intersections, so they form a base. Each $h(a)$ is open, and it is closed because its complement is $h(\neg a)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the Stone space $S(B)$ is compact with the ultrafilter theorem.
steps.detail: Suppose that basic sets $h(a_i)$ cover $S(B)$ but no finite subfamily does. Then every finite meet of the elements $\neg a_i$ is nonzero, so they generate a proper filter, and an ultrafilter that contains it lies in no $h(a_i)$, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Write every clopen set as a finite union of basic sets.
steps.detail: A [clopen](c:clopen-subset) set $C$ is closed in the [compact space](c:compact-space) $S(B)$, so it is compact. As an open set it is a union of basic sets, finitely many suffice, and $C = h(a_1 \vee \dots \vee a_n)$; with steps 1 and 2, $h$ is an isomorphism onto the clopen sets.

concepts.c:boolean-algebra: The algebra operations are what $h$ must preserve.
concepts.c:power-set: The field of sets lives inside the power set of $S(B)$.
concepts.c:ultrafilter: Ultrafilters are the points of the representing set.
concepts.c:clopen-subset: The image of $h$ is exactly the clopen sets.
concepts.c:stone-space: The Stone space is the compact space of ultrafilters with basic sets $h(a)$.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness makes every clopen set a finite union of basic sets.

source.note: The standard ultrafilter proof; M. H. Stone, The theory of representations for Boolean algebras, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 40 (1936), 37-111, gives it with prime ideals; see also Givant and Halmos, Introduction to Boolean Algebras (2009).

statement: For vectors $x, y$ of a real or complex [inner product space](c:inner-product-space), such as $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean [norm](c:norm), $\|x + y\| \le \|x\| + \|y\|$. Hence the distance $d(x, z) = \|x - z\|$ satisfies $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)$.

hypotheses.text: The space $E$ carries an inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ with [norm](c:norm) $\|x\| = \sqrt{\langle x, x \rangle}$.

conclusion: $\|x + y\| \le \|x\| + \|y\|$ and $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)$ for all $x, y, z \in E$.

formal.difference: The declaration states $\|a + b\| \le \|a\| + \|b\|$ in every seminormed group, where it follows from the triangle inequality of the distance, an axiom of that structure. This statement is the inner product case, in which the inequality needs a proof.

proofs.name: Square and Cauchy-Schwarz
proofs.slogan: Expand $\|x + y\|^2$, bound the cross term by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, and take square roots.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for real and complex scalars. The case $x = 0$ or $y = 0$ gives equality and needs no separate treatment.

roles.why: The inner product gives the expansion of the square and the Cauchy-Schwarz bound.

steps.slogan: Expand the square of the [norm](c:norm) of $x + y$.
steps.detail: Linearity and conjugate symmetry of the inner product give $\|x + y\|^2 = \langle x + y, x + y \rangle = \|x\|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}\langle x, y \rangle + \|y\|^2$.

steps.slogan: Bound the cross term $\operatorname{Re}\langle x, y \rangle$ by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
steps.detail: $\operatorname{Re}\langle x, y \rangle \le |\langle x, y \rangle| \le \|x\|\,\|y\|$. Substitution gives $\|x + y\|^2 \le \|x\|^2 + 2\|x\|\,\|y\| + \|y\|^2 = (\|x\| + \|y\|)^2$.

steps.slogan: Take square roots of the two nonnegative sides.
steps.detail: Both $\|x + y\|$ and $\|x\| + \|y\|$ are nonnegative, and $t \mapsto t^2$ is increasing on $[0, \infty)$. So the inequality of squares gives $\|x + y\| \le \|x\| + \|y\|$.

steps.slogan: Insert the middle point $y$ to get the triangle inequality for the distance.
steps.detail: Write $x - z = (x - y) + (y - z)$ and apply step 3: $d(x, z) \le \|x - y\| + \|y - z\| = d(x, y) + d(y, z)$. This is the axiom that makes $d$ a [metric](c:metric-space).

concepts.c:inner-product-space: The inner product gives the norm, the expansion and the Cauchy-Schwarz bound.
concepts.c:norm: The inequality compares norms of a sum and of its terms.
concepts.c:metric-space: The norm inequality gives the triangle axiom of the induced metric.

source.note: norm_add_le is dist_triangle for the distance of the norm; for an inner product space mathlib proves that inequality in InnerProductSpace.Core.toNormedAddCommGroup (add_le') by norm_inner_le_norm and a comparison of squares.

statement: Every irreducible positive-energy [unitary representation](c:unitary-representation) of the double cover of the [Poincaré group](c:poincare-group) is [induced](c:induced-representation) from a momentum orbit and an irreducible representation of its [stabilizer](c:stabilizer). Mass $m > 0$ adds a spin $s \in \frac12\mathbb{N}$, mass $0$ with $p \neq 0$ adds a helicity $h \in \frac12\mathbb{Z}$ or a continuous spin, and different data give inequivalent representations.

hypotheses.text: The representation $\pi$ is a strongly continuous, irreducible [unitary representation](c:unitary-representation) of $\widetilde{P} = \mathbb{R}^{1,3} \rtimes SL(2,\mathbb{C})$.
The joint spectrum of the translations, the energy-momentum, lies in the closed forward cone $p^0 \ge |\vec p|$.

conclusion: The representation $\pi$ is determined up to equivalence by its orbit and stabilizer data, and the list of these data has no repeats.

proofs.name: Mackey's little-group method
proofs.slogan: Restrict to the translations, find the momentum orbit that carries their spectrum, and induce from the stabilizer of a momentum on that orbit.
proofs.scope: An outline: the concentration of the spectrum on one orbit and the imprimitivity theorem rest on the cited work of Wigner and Mackey. The orbit $p = 0$ gives representations of $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ with trivial translations; the identification of particles with these representations is a physical postulate, not part of the theorem.

roles.why: Irreducibility makes the spectral measure ergodic and the inducing representation irreducible.
Positive energy keeps only the forward orbits and excludes the tachyonic hyperboloids.

steps.slogan: Restrict $\pi$ to the translation subgroup and take its joint spectral measure.
steps.detail: By the theorem of Stone, Naimark, Ambrose and Godement, the translations act as $\pi(a) = \int e^{i p \cdot a}\,dE(p)$ for a projection-valued measure $E$ on momentum space. Positive energy puts $E$ on the closed forward cone.

steps.slogan: Show that the spectral measure lives on one $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ [orbit](c:orbit) of momenta.
steps.detail: Covariance $\pi(g)E(S)\pi(g)^{-1} = E(gS)$ makes $E$ quasi-invariant, and irreducibility makes it ergodic. Each forward orbit is cut out by the value of $p^2$ and by whether $p = 0$, so an ergodic measure sits on one orbit.

steps.slogan: Recover $\pi$ as a representation [induced](c:induced-representation) from the stabilizer of one momentum.
steps.detail: The pair $(\pi, E)$ is a system of imprimitivity on the orbit. Mackey's imprimitivity theorem gives $\pi = \operatorname{Ind}(e^{ip \cdot a}\sigma)$ for an irreducible unitary $\sigma$ of the stabilizer $H_p$, and inequivalent $\sigma$ give inequivalent $\pi$.

steps.slogan: Compute the [stabilizer](c:stabilizer) of a momentum on each positive-energy orbit.
steps.detail: For $p = (m, 0, 0, 0)$ with $m > 0$ the stabilizer is $SU(2)$. For $p = (1, 0, 0, 1)$ it is the double cover of the Euclidean group $E(2)$, and for $p = 0$ it is all of $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$.

steps.slogan: List the irreducible unitary representations of each stabilizer to obtain the labels.
steps.detail: The irreducible unitary representations of $SU(2)$ are the spins $s \in \frac12\mathbb{N}$. Those of the cover of $E(2)$ are characters with helicity $h \in \frac12\mathbb{Z}$, or infinite-dimensional ones with a radius $\rho > 0$ and a sign, the continuous spins; with step 3 this gives the list without repeats.

concepts.c:unitary-representation: The objects classified are irreducible unitary representations.
concepts.c:poincare-group: The group is a semidirect product of translations and Lorentz transformations.
concepts.c:induced-representation: Every representation in the list is induced from a stabilizer.
concepts.c:stabilizer: The stabilizer of a momentum supplies the spin or helicity label.
concepts.c:orbit: The momentum orbit supplies the mass label.

source.ref: E. Wigner, On unitary representations of the inhomogeneous Lorentz group, Annals of Mathematics 40 (1939), no. 1, 149-204
source.note: Wigner found the list; G. W. Mackey, Induced representations of locally compact groups I, Annals of Mathematics 55 (1952), 101-139, supplies the imprimitivity theorem that makes the completeness proof rigorous.
